scheme: classical transliteration (accents omitted; rough breathing as h; iota subscript written as i)
en: Lord, the woman who had fallen into many sins,
perceiving your divinity, taking up the part of a myrrh-bearer,
lamenting, brings you myrrh before your burial.
"Alas!" she says, "for night is upon me, a frenzy of licentiousness,
dark and moonless, the love of sin.
Receive the springs of my tears,
you who by the clouds draw out the water of the sea;
bend to me, to the groanings of my heart,
you who bowed the heavens by your ineffable self-emptying.
I will kiss your spotless feet,
and wipe them again with the locks of my head,
whose footfall Eve in paradise, at evening,
having heard it sound in her ears, hid herself in fear.
The multitudes of my sins and the abysses of your judgements,
who will search them out, saviour of souls, my Saviour?
Do not disregard me, your handmaid, you who have mercy without measure."
rom: Kyrie, hē en pollais hamartiais peripesousa gynē,
tēn sēn aisthomenē theotēta, myrophorou analabousa taxin,
odyromenē, myra soi, pro tou entaphiasmou komizei.
Oimoi! legousa, hoti nyx moi hyparchei, oistros akolasias,
zophōdēs te kai aselēnos erōs tēs hamartias.
Dexai mou tas pēgas tōn dakryōn,
ho nephelais diexagōn tēs thalassēs to hydōr
kamphthēti moi pros tous stenagmous tēs kardias,
ho klinas tous ouranous tēi aphatōi sou kenōsei.
aposmēxō toutous de palin tois tēs kephalēs mou bostrychois
hōn en tōi paradeisōi Eua to deilinon,
kroton tois ōsin ēchētheisa, tōi phobōi ekrybē.
Hamartiōn mou ta plēthē kai krimatōn sou abyssous
Mē me tēn sēn doulēn paridēis, ho ametrēton echōn to eleos.
notes: Line 1.2: 'myrrh-bearer' (myrophoros) is the name given to the women who brought myrrh to anoint the body of Jesus.
Line 1.4: oistros akolasias, literally 'a gadfly (goad, frenzy) of licentiousness'.
Line 1.5: erōs tēs hamartias can be read as 'love of sin' or 'desire for sin'.
Line 1.7: diexagōn, 'drawing out' or 'leading through': the water of the sea is drawn up by the clouds.
Line 1.9: kenōsis, 'self-emptying', the theological term for God taking on human nature.
Lines 1.12-1.13: 'whose' (hōn) refers to the feet: Eve heard their footfall (kroton) in paradise in the evening and hid (Genesis 3:8). The Greek is one relative clause running over both lines.
Line 1.13: ēchētheisa, literally 'having been made to ring' in her ears with the sound.
Line 1.16: doulē, a female servant or slave; 'handmaid' in the biblical sense.
Line 1.15: the romanization keeps the Greek question mark ';' as written.
